name: Russian Violet
lede: Russian Violet is a near-black violet-purple recorded in the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930, so dark that it almost never turns up, as photographed, in our painting archive.

sections.title: A dark violet in the 1930 dictionary
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* records this hue in 1926, at plate 44, position K 11 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it in its "deep violet" block [1]. In Munsell notation it sits at about 1.4P 1.4 over 7.5, a near-black purple [1].

Our color library classes the name as a place-or-institution word, built on the adjective "Russian" [2]. Beyond the catalogue entry, the sources we hold say nothing about why that word was chosen for this particular violet; call the naming logic undocumented [2]. The two nearest named colors are [[adelaide]], about 5 units lighter, and [[midnight-purple]], a touch more vivid and darker, each within one step of Russian Violet in LCH space [3].

Two further neighbors sit a little further off: [[midnight-purple]], darker and more vivid, and [[paua]], at 6 units, also darker [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Russian Violet is close to black, so near-black that it barely appears in paintings at all [4]. Our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, finds a color within six units of it covering at least five per cent of a canvas exactly once, in Édouard Manet's *Bullfight* of 1865, where it covers about nine per cent of the canvas [4]. By century, that one hit falls in the 1800s, at nearly three times the rate you would expect by chance across the whole archive, and works from France carry the color at nearly seven times the archive's overall rate [4]. Every one of those few matches reads as a shadow, never a highlight or a mid-tone [4]. The caveat is the usual one: these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen color, not a pigment identification [4].
